title: No signs of AI payoff outside the tech sector
content:
Marc Rowan on how Apollo’s differentiated strategy was built for this moment.
October 24, 2026
No Signs of AI Payoff Outside the Tech Sector
Despite massive investments and widespread hype around artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech. Revenue per worker is rising for the Mag 7 but is flat for the S&P 493, see the first chart below. Profit margins are rising for the Mag 7 but are flat for the S&P 493, see the second chart below. And there are still no signs of AI boosting productivity growth, see the third chart below. With no impact on the bottom line, mainstream corporate America is pulling back and starting to view token spending not as a source of growth but as a cost center that weighs on margins.
VC-backed companies are spending more and more on tokens, but mainstream corporate America does not need the latest model and is unwilling to pay for it. As long as agentic AI and token spending are confined to a small part of the economy, the macroeconomic effects of AI will be very limited, see the fourth and fifth charts below.
The question looking ahead is whether, even as models become commoditized, mainstream corporate America can turn increasingly cheap intelligence into higher revenue growth and higher profit margins. That may be harder than it sounds. AI may be a great calculator, but in business, intelligence is mostly judgment. Judgment depends on context, and the answer varies with which human or which model you ask. Perhaps most importantly, AI does not understand accountability, trust, culture, unwritten rules, ethical trade-offs or fairness, all of which shape reputational risk and ultimately drive revenue growth and profit margins.
The bottom line is that the AI story will be decided in the S&P 493, not the Mag 7, and so far, there is no evidence that revenue growth or margins are improving outside the tech sector.

report.summary: Apollo analysis finds AI investment and hype have not yet boosted revenue, margins, or productivity outside the tech sector, where token spending is increasingly seen as a cost.
report.background: The AI boom has been driven by massive capex from hyperscalers and the Magnificent Seven, plus venture-backed startups consuming tokens. But corporate adoption outside tech is uneven: most firms are testing tools rather than rebuilding workflows. Investors are asking when AI spending will show up in earnings. Historically, general-purpose technologies take time to diffuse, and productivity gains require complementary changes in process, data, and skills. The article argues that as long as agentic AI and token spending remain concentrated in a small slice of the economy, macroeconomic effects will be limited, and the real test will be whether cheap intelligence can lift revenue and margins across the S&P 493.
key_points: Performance is split. Revenue per worker and profit margins are rising for the Magnificent Seven but flat for the S&P 493. That suggests AI gains are concentrated in tech rather than spreading across the broader corporate sector.

Productivity has not visibly improved. Despite heavy investment and hype, the article finds no signs that AI is boosting aggregate productivity growth. That undercuts the case that AI is already transforming how mainstream companies operate.

Mainstream firms treat tokens as a cost. Outside tech, companies say they do not need the latest model and are unwilling to pay for it. Token spending is increasingly viewed as a cost center that weighs on margins, prompting pullback.

Macro impact is limited while adoption is narrow. VC-backed startups spend heavily on tokens, but mainstream corporate America does not. As long as agentic AI and token spending stay confined to a small part of the economy, the macroeconomic effects will be modest.

Cheap intelligence is not enough. In business, intelligence is mostly judgment shaped by context, accountability, trust, culture, unwritten rules, ethics, and fairness. AI can calculate, but it does not understand these factors, which drive reputational risk and ultimately revenue and margins.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the article shifts the burden of proof from capability demos to measurable ROI outside tech. Model vendors may face pricing pressure and commoditization, while winners will be those that package AI into workflow-specific products with clear cost savings. Developers should focus less on raw model access and more on context, evaluations, observability, accountability, and integration with business judgment. Regular users may see more cautious AI rollouts and tighter budgets for AI features, with benefits concentrated among tech firms and startups for now. If cheap intelligence does not translate into revenue or margins, the next wave of AI spending could be slower and more selective.
report.tools: To follow the ROI debate, watch AI cost and observability tools such as Helicone and Langfuse, evaluation frameworks like promptfoo and Ragas, and workflow/agent platforms such as LangGraph and CrewAI. Open-source models (Llama, Mistral, Qwen) matter because commoditized, cheaper inference is central to the article’s thesis. For enterprise ROI tracking, pair these with OpenTelemetry-based monitoring and finance dashboards that attribute token spend to business outcomes.
